opener.label: Before any algebra
opener.display: I square my number and get 12 more than the number itself.

steps.say: A guess-the-number puzzle, no algebra needed. I am thinking of a number. When I square it, I get 12 more than the number I started with.
steps.hint: Try 4: four squared is 16, and 16 is 12 more than 4.

steps.say: Good. There is a second number that also works, and it is negative.
steps.hint: Try −3: negative three squared is 9, and 9 is 12 more than −3.

steps.say: You just solved \(x^2 = x + 12\) and found BOTH answers, \(x = 4\) and \(x = -3\). That is the whole topic: an equation with a square in it usually has TWO answers. In algebra it appears as a line \(y = x + 12\) crossing a curve \(y = x^2\); they meet at two points, so there are two x-values to find.
Both equations give y, so set the two right sides equal: \(x + 3 = x^2 - 3\). Bring every term to the right so \(x^2\) stays positive.

steps.hint: The line's +x moves across to become −x.
The +3 crosses to −3, and −3 stays, so −3 − 3.

steps.say: So \(x^2 - x - 6 = 0\). Two numbers multiply to −6 and add to −1: they are −3 and 2, giving \((x - 3)(x + 2) = 0\).
Now each x gets its y from \(y = x + 3\).

steps.done: It equals y = 6, so (3, 6) is right and (−2, 1) checks the same way.

steps.say: Set the two right sides equal: \(2x - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 4\). There are x-terms and numbers on both sides, so move everything to the right with care.
Each x gets its y from \(y = 2x - 1\).

steps.done: It equals y = 9, so (5, 9) is right and (1, 1) checks the same way.

steps.say: The second equation is a circle. Rearrange the line \(x + y = 6\) to \(y = 6 - x\). Substitute into \(x^2 + y^2 = 20\): \(x^2 + (6 - x)^2 = 20\). Expand \((6 - x)^2 = 36 - 12x + x^2\).
steps.hint: 2 times 6 is 12, and it is negative.

steps.say: So \(2x^2 - 12x + 16 = 0\). Divide every term by 2 to get \(x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0\), which factorises as \((x - 2)(x - 4) = 0\).
Each x gets its y from \(y = 6 - x\).

steps.done: It equals 20, so (2, 4) is right and (4, 2) checks the same way.

method_card.title: Simultaneous Equations (One Linear, One Quadratic)
steps: Rearrange the linear equation to make one letter the subject.
Substitute it into the quadratic, expanding any bracket in full.
Rearrange to a quadratic equal to zero, then factorise or use the formula.
Substitute each x back into the linear equation for its y, and give both pairs.
method_card.content:
When one equation is a straight line and the other is a curve (a quadratic, or a circle \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\)), use substitution. The line usually crosses the curve at two points, so expect two pairs of answers.

Make a letter the subject of the line, substitute it in, and simplify to a quadratic equal to zero. Solve it, then find each matching value from the line. Always give answers as pairs.
method_card.example:
Solve \(y = x + 1\) and \(y = x^2 - 1\)

\(x + 1 = x^2 - 1 \Rightarrow x^2 - x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 2)(x + 1) = 0\), so \(x = 2\) or \(x = -1\). Then \(y = 3\) or \(y = 0\): the pairs are \((2, 3)\) and \((-1, 0)\).

bronze.title: Bronze: substitute, factorise, two answers
steps: Both equations are written as y = …, so set the two right-hand sides equal to each other.
Move every term to one side to get a quadratic equal to zero, then factorise it.
Each bracket gives one x-value. Put each x back into the linear equation to find its y.

silver.title: Silver: rearrange first, then substitute
steps: The linear part may be \(y = 2x - 1\), \(x + y = 5\), or \(xy = 10\); rearrange it to make one letter the subject first.
Substitute, expand any bracket in full, and gather x-terms and numbers from both sides.
Factorise the quadratic, then find each y from the linear equation.

gold.title: Gold: circles and the quadratic formula
steps: For a circle \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\), rearrange the line to \(y = …\) and substitute, squaring the bracket in full.
\((a - x)^2 = a^2 - 2ax + x^2\): never square the two terms separately.
If the quadratic will not factorise, use the formula and give the two x-values as asked.
